title: Innovation Lessons for Product Managers: Balancing the Here and Now and the Future
content:
The Grass Is Always Greener — and What That Teaches Us

There is a pattern that plays out across every type of organisation. Consultants believe large companies have everything they need to execute. Startups dream of the resources and reach of large corporations. And those inside large organisations envy the speed and agility of startups. The cows in the calming slide are there for a reason: we always think the grass is greener on the other side. But the most important innovation lessons come precisely from moving across all three contexts — consultancy, startup, and corporate — and recognising what each genuinely offers.

Working across these environments, certain patterns repeat. The first is that inspiration matters more than motivation. The second is that structure drives behaviour more than culture alone. And the third is that falling in love with the problem — rather than the solution — is what separates durable innovation from clever but short-lived ideas. Three books crystallise these lessons: Start With Why by Simon Sinek, Loonshots by Safi Bahcall, and The Lean Product Playbook by Dan Olsen.

Start With Why: Fall in Love With the Problem

Sinek's core argument is straightforward: to get people to join you in uncertainty, you need to inspire them — not just motivate them. And inspiration comes from understanding and communicating why you are doing something, not what you are building or how you are building it. This is not merely a communication technique. It is a discipline for product teams, because the act of articulating the why forces you to confront whether you have understood the problem at all.

A concrete example: working on a project to detect early-stage Parkinson's disease through voice analysis. A phone call, a brief recording, and an algorithm could flag neurological changes years before a formal diagnosis. The technical results were encouraging — a 78% reliability rate on the initial prototype. The team believed they were doing something genuinely important. They tested prototypes in pharmacies. They validated the hypothesis that health organisations would want to screen large numbers of people.

But asking why — and asking it five times over — led somewhere unexpected. Early diagnosis of Parkinson's is only valuable if there is something to be done with that diagnosis. At the time, medication could manage symptoms but could not slow the disease. Telling someone they have early-stage Parkinson's, when you cannot offer meaningful intervention, creates anxiety without relief. The question "why are we really doing this?" revealed that the project's underlying logic was flawed. The team closed it down. That is what it means to fall in love with the problem rather than the solution.

Loonshots: Phase Separation and the Ambidextrous Organisation

Safi Bahcall's Loonshots draws a surprising analogy between water and organisations. Water can exist as ice or liquid; the transition between states is determined not by changing the molecules themselves, but by changing the conditions — temperature, pressure. Organisations work the same way. You do not change culture by changing people one by one. You change structure, and behaviour follows.

Bahcall's central insight is that innovation and execution require fundamentally different conditions, and successful organisations must maintain both simultaneously — what he calls phase separation. The history of radar illustrates this well. The underlying science was available for decades. A German engineer, Christian Hülsmeyer, demonstrated the basic principle as early as 1904, detecting ships through fog using reflected radio waves. Yet it took until the Second World War — and the creation of a dedicated research structure, the Office of Scientific Research and Development under Vannevar Bush — to turn that science into a deployable military technology.

The US Navy's early reluctance is instructive: they were uninterested in any project that would take more than three years. That constraint — entirely rational from an execution standpoint — is precisely the constraint that kills early-stage innovation. The lesson is not that large organisations are incompetent; it is that they are optimised for delivery, not discovery. The ambidextrous organisation creates deliberate structural separation: one part runs the business, another bets on the future, and the two operate under different rules.

The Lean Product Playbook: Hypothesis-Driven Development

Dan Olsen's framework offers the practical counterpart to the strategic lessons above. The core discipline is deceptively simple: before building anything, write down your hypothesis. Define what you believe to be true, who you believe will benefit, and what observable outcome would tell you whether you are right. Then design the smallest possible test of that hypothesis.

This sounds obvious. It rarely gets done. The Parkinson's project is again instructive: the hypothesis was that health organisations would want to identify undiagnosed patients at scale. The test — a prototype screening kiosk placed in pharmacies — was lightweight and fast. The insight it produced (that early detection without effective treatment creates more problems than it solves) was not the insight the team expected. But it was the right insight, and it came cheaply.

The hypothesis card discipline works because it forces specificity. "We believe X" is not a hypothesis. "We believe that pharmacies serving populations over 50 will pay for a screening device if it takes under two minutes per patient and delivers results within 48 hours" is a hypothesis. The more specific the claim, the clearer the test, and the faster the learning. Combined with a genuine understanding of why you are doing the work and a structure that protects early-stage ideas from execution-stage pressures, hypothesis-driven development gives teams the best possible chance of building something that actually matters.

Putting the Lessons Together

The three lessons reinforce each other. Start with why grounds the work in a genuine problem worth solving. Phase separation ensures that promising ideas are not killed by short-term performance pressure before they have had a chance to develop. And the lean hypothesis discipline ensures that the development process itself generates real learning rather than just confirmation of existing assumptions.

None of this is easy in practice. Large organisations resist structural separation because it looks like inefficiency. Startups resist the discipline of hypothesis testing because speed feels like a substitute for rigour. Consultancies resist falling in love with problems because clients pay for solutions. But the organisations — and the product leaders — who manage to hold all three lessons simultaneously are the ones who build things that last.
